what_its_for: Panitumumab is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum) that has spread to other parts of the body. It works by blocking a protein called EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) that helps cancer cells grow. It is used in patients whose cancer has a normal (wild-type) RAS gene.
how_to_take: Panitumumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion directly into your vein by a healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital setting. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes about 60 minutes. You will be monitored closely during and after each infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight. The typical dose is 6 mg per kilogram (mg/kg) of body weight, given once every 2 weeks. Your doctor may slow down, pause, or permanently stop your infusion if you have a reaction. Never try to adjust your dose on your own.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider at a clinic, a missed appointment is unlikely. However, if you need to reschedule or miss your infusion appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to make up the dose on your own.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. Your healthcare provider stores and prepares it for you. If you are ever given information about storing it, keep it refrigerated at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C), protected from light, and do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid prolonged sun exposure while taking this medicine, as it can make your skin very sensitive to sunlight. Wear protective clothing, hats, and sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) whenever you go outside. Avoid smoking, as it may reduce how well the medicine works. Tell your doctor before taking any new medicines, vitamins, or supplements. Avoid becoming pregnant during treatment, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: severe skin rash, blistering, peeling, or sores in your mouth; difficulty breathing, wheezing, or chest tightness during or after your infusion; swelling of your face, lips, or throat; severe diarrhea or dehydration; eye redness, irritation, or pain; signs of low magnesium such as muscle cramps, irregular heartbeat, or seizures; any signs of serious infection such as fever or chills. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Panitumumab does not cure cancer but can help slow its growth or shrink tumors. Some patients begin to see benefits after a few treatment cycles, but it may take several weeks to months before your doctor can tell how well the medicine is working. Your doctor will check your progress with regular tests and scans.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can harm your unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 2 months after your last dose. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine and for at least 2 months after your last dose, as it may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Older adults: Older patients may use this medicine but should be watched closely for side effects. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver problems before starting treatment.
